classification_signals: Expanded second edition reviewing new findings (p. 2)
Discussing key biometric tools and suggesting new ways to analyze designs (p. 2)
Includes a new chapter on using biometrics (p. 2)
Includes 'Case Study' sections (e.g., Palmer Square, Columbia, Main Street Disneyland, Oval Office, Kelley's Corner, Gropius House) (p. 33, 36, 42, 115, 130, 180)
Chapter 7: 'Buildings, Biology + Biometrics: Collecting Empirical Data for Evidence-Based Design' (p. 8)
Reports on 'eye-tracking studies' and presents 'heat maps' and 'gaze paths' (p. 177-194)
Proposes 'A New Foundation' and 'The Twenty-First-Century Paradigm Shift' (p. 8, 169)
title: Cognitive Architecture: Designing for How We Respond to the Built Environment, Second Edition
authors: Ann Sussman and Justin B. Hollander, 2021

findings.antecedent: Understanding human evolution and biology
findings.consequent: Creativity and success in architectural design and planning
findings.source: A New Foundation: Darwin, Biology, and Cognitive Science, p. 28
findings.quote: The thesis of this book is that the more we understand how human beings are an artifact of Darwin’s theory of evolution, the more creatively and successfully we will be able to design and plan for them.

findings.antecedent: Human perceptual systems evolved in natural environments
findings.consequent: Mismatch with modern man-made built environments
findings.source: A New Foundation: Darwin, Biology, and Cognitive Science, p. 29
findings.quote: Our perceptual systems are designed to register aspects of the external world that were important to our survival …

findings.antecedent: Open urban spaces (center) vs. sides of streets/edges
findings.consequent: Human movement and preference
findings.source: Edges Matter: Thigmotaxis (the ‘Wall-hugging’ Trait), p. 30
findings.quote: people avoid the center of open spaces and tend to stick to the sides of streets, even in car-free zones.

findings.antecedent: Environmental edges/walls
findings.consequent: Thigmotactic behavior (wall-hugging), anxiety levels, spatial learning
findings.source: Edges Matter: Thigmotaxis (the ‘Wall-hugging’ Trait), p. 47
findings.quote: thigmotactic behavior, which is relatively easy to follow and measure, increases with anxiety and decreases with familiarity

findings.antecedent: Continuous edges and street corridors
findings.consequent: Aided human movement, effortless stroll
findings.source: Edges Matter: Thigmotaxis (the ‘Wall-hugging’ Trait), p. 41
findings.quote: It turns out continuous edges and street corridors aid and abet our movement, and this is an artifact of our evolution

findings.antecedent: Edward W. Brooke Courthouse arcade (tall, wide piers, impedes views, no human scale)
findings.consequent: Difficult navigation, increased psychological arousal, energy-intensive movement
findings.source: Edges Matter: Thigmotaxis (the ‘Wall-hugging’ Trait), p. 9 (caption) & p. 51
findings.quote: The arcade of the Edward W Brooke Court House in Boston (1999, Kalmann McKinnell and Wood) does not acknowledge the way people like to walk, inadvertently promoting confusion in the urban landscape.

findings.antecedent: Rue de Rivoli arcade (Paris), medieval street (Siena) (human scale, directs movement, continuous edges)
findings.consequent: Reassuring walking path, effortless stroll, reduced uncertainty
findings.source: Edges Matter: Thigmotaxis (the ‘Wall-hugging’ Trait), p. 51
findings.quote: The Parisian structure provides a reassuring walking path. It takes much of the uncertainty and guesswork out of walking in a large city. Everything seems so simple here.

findings.antecedent: Columbia, Maryland's urban design (curvilinear roads, few intersections, open landscapes, lack of street wall)
findings.consequent: Difficult pedestrian navigation, feelings of being lost, reduced walkability
findings.source: Edges Matter: Thigmotaxis (the ‘Wall-hugging’ Trait), p. 65
findings.quote: Even though there are sidewalks in Columbia, the open landscapes around them provide little in the way of a street wall, making it difficult for people to figure out where they are and which way to head. Pedestrians and even newcomers traveling by car perennially feel lost in Columbia.

findings.antecedent: Indoor shopping malls (double-loaded corridors, stores on both sides)
findings.consequent: Successful commercial spaces, increased engagement/buying
findings.source: Edges Matter: Thigmotaxis (the ‘Wall-hugging’ Trait), p. 58
findings.quote: Given our edge-sensitivity, it becomes easier to understand why indoor shopping malls can be successful, because they often duplicate the plan of an old-fashioned commercial street.

findings.antecedent: Disneyland's Main Street (narrow, car-free, detailed facades, forced-perspective, face-like elements)
findings.consequent: Visitor orientation, sense of security, positive movement, emotional attachment
findings.source: Edges Matter: Thigmotaxis (the ‘Wall-hugging’ Trait), p. 72
findings.quote: It seems Disney intuited modern research on thigmotaxis, and also knew that a carefully detailed row of colorful shops would not only entertain but also help visitors situate themselves, feel secure inside the gates, and propel them on through the park in a happy frame of mind.

findings.antecedent: Human brain's visual processing
findings.consequent: Prioritization of faces, emotional impact of portraits
findings.source: Patterns Matter: Faces and Spaces, p. 30 & p. 77
findings.quote: More of our gray matter is devoted to creating our visual representation of the world than anything else... Moreover, our mental apparatus does not handle visual inputs equally either—it prioritizes the face.

findings.antecedent: Upright vs. inverted faces
findings.consequent: Facial recognition ability
findings.source: Patterns Matter: Faces and Spaces, p. 79
findings.quote: The evidence clearly indicates that the ability to encode faces is present very early in life,’ particularly, when presented right-side up, writes scientist Elinor McKone and her colleagues. ‘Babies discriminate faces upright but fail to discriminate the same stimuli inverted’ (p. 7).

findings.antecedent: Faces vs. other objects
findings.consequent: FFA activation
findings.source: Patterns Matter: Faces and Spaces, p. 80
findings.quote: This region, the FFA, ‘responds more strongly to faces than objects’ (Kanwisher et al. 1997: 4308).

findings.antecedent: Random visual data
findings.consequent: Perception of faces (pareidolia), evolutionary advantage
findings.source: Patterns Matter: Faces and Spaces, p. 86
findings.quote: The human brain’s adeptness at processing faces appears to contribute to quirks in our perception where we easily see faces in places they are not. We find faces in clouds, the moon, a tortilla chip, or the burnt markings on a piece of toast. This phenomenon is called pareidolia

findings.antecedent: Face-like inanimate objects
findings.consequent: Emotional engagement, visual processing, memory
findings.source: Patterns Matter: Faces and Spaces, p. 88
findings.quote: It turns out ‘we process these ‘fake’ faces using the same visual mechanisms of the brain that we do for real ones,’ a report on the research explains (Gilbert 2020).

findings.antecedent: Building facades with face-like features ('face-i-tecture')
findings.consequent: Increased attention, emotional engagement, memorability, aesthetic preference
findings.source: Patterns Matter: Faces and Spaces, p. 93
findings.quote: What about buildings? Not surprisingly, a building designed to look like a face grabs our attention and can hook our emotions much like a billboard papered with one does.

findings.antecedent: Distance to another human
findings.consequent: Visual perception of human features (detection, body language, facial expression)
findings.source: Patterns Matter: Faces and Spaces, p. 103
findings.quote: Only when the distance has been reduced to about 100 meters (110 yards) can we see movement and body language in broad outline. Gender and age can be identified as the pedestrian approaches, and we usually recognize the person at somewhere between 50 and 70 meters (55 and 75 yards) … At a distance of about 22 to 25 meters (24–27 yards) we can accurately read facial expression and dominant emotions.

findings.antecedent: Civic space dimensions (within 100m radius vs. larger/amorphous)
findings.consequent: Social engagement, recognition of others, avoidance
findings.source: Patterns Matter: Faces and Spaces, p. 106 (caption) & p. 106
findings.quote: Piazza del Campo, the popular medieval square in Siena, Italy makes for a great civic and social space. A resident walking into its center is likely to easily find and recognize a friend or acquaintance in the same space.

findings.antecedent: Visual field/viewport (3/2 ratio)
findings.consequent: Processing fluency for similarly shaped objects/media
findings.source: Patterns Matter: Faces and Spaces, p. 113 (caption) & p. 115 (caption)
findings.quote: The human viewport, evolving for fast horizontal scanning, approximates a rectangle of 3/2 proportions

findings.antecedent: Bilateral symmetry, curves, organized complexity in environment
findings.consequent: Preference, faster mental processing, feelings of happiness/elation, reduced stress
findings.source: Shapes Carry Weight: Bilateral Symmetry, (Hierarchy), Curves, and Complexity, p. 124
findings.quote: Shapes carry weight. We do not look out at the world around us as though all things are equal. We have evolved to register and investigate and prefer certain forms over others in fractions of a second.

findings.antecedent: Bilateral symmetry in forms
findings.consequent: Perception of power/prestige, evolutionary advantage (motion, senses, brain development)
findings.source: Shapes Carry Weight: Bilateral Symmetry, (Hierarchy), Curves, and Complexity, p. 133
findings.quote: Bilateral symmetry conveys significant advantages for its species, including us. The form is ranked as ‘an important advance’ because ‘it opened the way for the development of directed motion, improved organs of sense and, eventually, the enlarged and highly complex mammalian brain’ (Prosser 2012).

findings.antecedent: Symmetrical vs. asymmetrical faces/designs
findings.consequent: Aesthetic preference, perceived health/fitness
findings.source: Shapes Carry Weight: Bilateral Symmetry, (Hierarchy), Curves, and Complexity, p. 135
findings.quote: Men and women find symmetrical faces more attractive than non-symmetrical ones, research has confirmed. ‘Preference for symmetry, while perhaps acquirable through cultural processes, is rooted in our evolutionary history,’ a recent paper in the field noted (Cárdenas and Harris 2006: 3).

findings.antecedent: Vertical bilateral symmetry vs. other symmetries
findings.consequent: Speed of visual processing
findings.source: Shapes Carry Weight: Bilateral Symmetry, (Hierarchy), Curves, and Complexity, p. 137
findings.quote: Psychologists studying symmetry perception have found that people process vertical bilateral symmetry (oriented around the vertical axis), in objects more quickly than other forms of repetition or symmetry

findings.antecedent: Symmetrical objects
findings.consequent: Smiling muscle activation, feelings of calm/reassurance
findings.source: Shapes Carry Weight: Bilateral Symmetry, (Hierarchy), Curves, and Complexity, p. 137
findings.quote: Researchers have also learned that looking at symmetrical objects activates our smiling muscles more than looking at random patterns (Makin et al. 2012: 3255). And when we smile, we are more likely to feel calm or reassured.

findings.antecedent: Curved vs. angular/sharp shapes
findings.consequent: Emotional response (happiness/elation vs. pain/sadness)
findings.source: Shapes Carry Weight: Bilateral Symmetry, (Hierarchy), Curves, and Complexity, p. 138
findings.quote: curves elicit feelings of happiness and elation, while jagged and sharp forms tend to connect to feelings of pain and sadness

findings.antecedent: Repetitive parallel lines in building facades
findings.consequent: Brain stress, increased oxygen uptake (visual cortex), reduced visual comfort
findings.source: Shapes Carry Weight: Bilateral Symmetry, (Hierarchy), Curves, and Complexity, p. 141-142
findings.quote: Researchers have found that as more and more stripes in building facades appear decade by decade, the buildings become less and less comfortable to look at (Wilkins 2018).

findings.antecedent: Oval Office design (rounded walls, bilateral symmetry)
findings.consequent: Psychological advantage, positive emotional response, sense of power
findings.source: Shapes Carry Weight: Bilateral Symmetry, (Hierarchy), Curves, and Complexity, p. 142
findings.quote: Our bias toward curves suggests why the design of the ‘Oval Office,’ the traditional seat of power of the American president, may carry a psychological advantage for its occupant; not only is it bilaterally symmetrical with the desk centered on its longer axis, indicative of psychological power, but its rounded walls are of an innately preferred shape

findings.antecedent: Environmental complexity (too simple, middle, too complex)
findings.consequent: Emotional/cognitive response (boredom, satisfaction, confusion), preference
findings.source: Shapes Carry Weight: Bilateral Symmetry, (Hierarchy), Curves, and Complexity, p. 144
findings.quote: Psychologists have demonstrated that people prefer a middle level of complexity: too simple and we are bored, too complex and we are confused. Moreover, the ideal level of complexity is a moving target, because the more expert we become at any subject, the more complexity we prefer.

findings.antecedent: Organized complexity vs. randomness in environment
findings.consequent: Survival, homeostasis, sensory processing efficiency, brain energy use
findings.source: Shapes Carry Weight: Bilateral Symmetry, (Hierarchy), Curves, and Complexity, p. 145
findings.quote: Organized complexity is so important, in the end, because it promotes survival, helping the body efficiently maintain a state of homeostasis or equilibrium (Salingaros 2021).

findings.antecedent: Fractal patterns (not too dense/sparse) in nature and art
findings.consequent: Aesthetic appeal, relaxation, alpha response in frontal region
findings.source: Shapes Carry Weight: Bilateral Symmetry, (Hierarchy), Curves, and Complexity, p. 146
findings.quote: Humans appear to have innate preferences for fractal patterns that are not too dense, but not too sparse, Taylor reports, re-iterating points Norman and Salingaros make. Patterns in the ideal range ‘generated the maximal alpha response in the frontal region, consistent with the hypothesis that they are most relaxing,’ he explains (Taylor et al. 2011: 18).

findings.antecedent: Human narrative capacity
findings.consequent: Sense of self, connection to environment, adaptive behavior, imaginative work
findings.source: Storytelling Is Key: We’re Wired for Narrative, p. 149
findings.quote: Just as the human brain is primed to find faces, favors symmetry, and enjoys ordered complexity, it runs on narrative. How we see our world and how we see ourselves ultimately involves a story.

findings.antecedent: Spatial sequencing/narrative in design (e.g., Frank Lloyd Wright's houses, Villa Lante)
findings.consequent: Enjoyment of place, connection to place, sense of arrival, dignity
findings.source: Storytelling Is Key: We’re Wired for Narrative, p. 151
findings.quote: Frank Lloyd Wright’s house plans, for example, are known for their clear sequencing: a small entryway with a low ceiling leads to a tight anteroom and then crescendos in the large public living space with high ceiling, a fireplace (‘the hearth’), and a broad view of nature outside (see Figure 5.1).

findings.antecedent: Urban design (lack of narrative/scattered vs. clear hierarchy/narrative)
findings.consequent: Feelings of placelessness/anomie vs. pride of place/positive identity
findings.source: Storytelling Is Key: We’re Wired for Narrative, p. 157 & p. 159
findings.quote: The sprawling entry point, called Kelley’s Corner, is a short distance from the public school campus, and has been a source of embarrassment for townspeople for more than three decades.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to nature/natural scenes (especially savanna-like)
findings.consequent: Innate preference, emotional well-being, health
findings.source: Nature Is Our Context: Biophilia and Biophilic Design, p. 163
findings.quote: We have an innate ‘tendency to focus on life and lifelike processes,’ biologist E. O. Wilson explains in his 1984 book Biophilia (p. 1).

findings.antecedent: Exposure to nature (real, painted, photographed)
findings.consequent: Reduced stress, faster hospital recovery, less pain medicine, enhanced cognitive abilities, increased happiness/well-being
findings.source: Nature Is Our Context: Biophilia and Biophilic Design, p. 168
findings.quote: Studies show that experiencing nature and its visual complexity, even for a few minutes, even represented in a painting or photograph, reduces stress and has other benefits.

findings.antecedent: High levels of greenery (tree plantings) in urban/prison environments
findings.consequent: Perceived health, social interactions, supervision of children, mental health, cognitive functioning, learning, reduced recidivism
findings.source: Nature Is Our Context: Biophilia and Biophilic Design, p. 169
findings.quote: high levels of greenery in an urban area is correlated with perception of health... Planting trees in public housing ‘increased opportunities for social interactions, monitoring of outdoor areas, and supervision of children’

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design (incorporating natural elements, forms, patterns, light, place-based relationships)
findings.consequent: Improved community health/well-being, emotional attachment to place, sustainability
findings.source: Nature Is Our Context: Biophilia and Biophilic Design, p. 167
findings.quote: The green movement cannot achieve its goal of sustainability, Kellert elaborated, because it fell short of nurturing the physical and benefits that create emotional attachment to place in the first place, which motivates people to care for their constructions and retain them over the long term (Kellert 2012: 162).

findings.antecedent: Use of biometric tools (eye tracking, facial expression analysis, EEG, GSR)
findings.consequent: Visibility of unconscious behaviors, understanding/prediction of human responses, improved design
findings.source: Buildings, Biology + Biometrics: Collecting Empirical Data for Evidence-Based Design, p. 173-174
findings.quote: How we can get hard data on our unconscious behavior and our actual physical responses as we experience buildings is the subject of this chapter. It helps us ‘see’ who we are, reviewing tools that reveal the ‘unseen,’ and changes our understanding of how architecture impacts people and gives designers and planners new terms to describe the human experience

findings.antecedent: Building facades with windows vs. without windows
findings.consequent: Visual fixation duration on facade, memory formation of place
findings.source: Buildings, Biology + Biometrics: Collecting Empirical Data for Evidence-Based Design, p. 178 & p. 179
findings.quote: In a 15-second testing interval (Figure 7.2), the brain made viewers focus on the entire facade with windows, and effectively ignore the building, save its door, when it did not have them.

findings.antecedent: Blank facades vs. facades with windows/contrast
findings.consequent: Visual attention/engagement, heat map intensity
findings.source: Buildings, Biology + Biometrics: Collecting Empirical Data for Evidence-Based Design, p. 180
findings.quote: We again found that blank facades got little attention and that discrete areas of contrast, even on a high-rise tower a block away, instantly drew the eye (Figure 7.6).

findings.antecedent: Large glass facade vs. people/high-contrast elements
findings.consequent: Visual attention/fixation
findings.source: Buildings, Biology + Biometrics: Collecting Empirical Data for Evidence-Based Design, p. 183
findings.quote: Eye tracking reveals that people barely gave the enormous glass façade here a glance, despite its size. It is the white-contrasting bus roof, the people, both real and in advertisements and banners, that caught their eye in the scene, along with the red traffic light and flag (Figure 7.9).

findings.antecedent: Human form vs. skyscraper
findings.consequent: Visual attention/fixation, heat map intensity
findings.source: Buildings, Biology + Biometrics: Collecting Empirical Data for Evidence-Based Design, p. 184
findings.quote: Guess what detail grabbed viewers’ attention most? If you chose the small silhouette of the floating man on a raft, you are right... when it comes to the human form, the brain couldn’t help but go for it, creating the reddest heat map around him. Otherwise, people hardly looked at the skyscraper

findings.antecedent: Presence vs. absence of distant landmark (water tower)
findings.consequent: Visual orientation, attention focus, perceived ease of movement
findings.source: Buildings, Biology + Biometrics: Collecting Empirical Data for Evidence-Based Design, p. 185 & p. 186
findings.quote: Eye tracking both images shows how people on the bridge instinctively use the tower as a prime orientation point (Figure 7.12).

findings.antecedent: Building facade with windows vs. without windows
findings.consequent: Time to first fixation (TTFF) on door, visual fixation pattern
findings.source: Buildings, Biology + Biometrics: Collecting Empirical Data for Evidence-Based Design, p. 186
findings.quote: The image at left shows the TTFF (or Time to First Fixation) is 0.9 seconds for the door. It takes just a fraction-of-a-second longer to find the door when the library has windows, TTFF: 1.2 seconds, see image at right. However, without windows, by the second fixation (TTFF: 12.6 s) almost half of viewers focus beyond the building (Ratio: 12/30). With windows, the brain does not let this happen. Note how fixations 2, 3, and 5 keep people focusing back on the front facade.

findings.antecedent: Blank concrete wall vs. wall with art
findings.consequent: Visual fixation pattern, perceived appeal
findings.source: Buildings, Biology + Biometrics: Collecting Empirical Data for Evidence-Based Design, p. 188
findings.quote: The heat map shows the biggest, reddest dots at its edges, suggesting the first thing people do arriving at the Davis stop is literally avoid looking at what greets them. Add a design intervention, however, such as a blue Matisse-like art to the blank concrete, and behavior shifts; people will fixate in the center of the wall (image at top right) no longer paying as much attention to its edges.

findings.antecedent: Car-centric suburban subdivision vs. new urbanist street (denser, aligned residences)
findings.consequent: Gaze path (skyward vs. street level), walkability
findings.source: Buildings, Biology + Biometrics: Collecting Empirical Data for Evidence-Based Design, p. 192-193
findings.quote: typical streets in U.S.-car-centric-subdivisions, such as at left, make viewers implicitly look straight ahead and then skyward, up at trees (Hollander et al. 2021a). ... New urbanist or more old-fashioned housing on the right, however, ... produces the opposite, a gaze path along the street, following the building edges, directing the viewer to stay focused at grade level.

findings.antecedent: New Art Center vs. sculpture at entrance/old commercial building
findings.consequent: Visual attention/fixation
findings.source: Buildings, Biology + Biometrics: Collecting Empirical Data for Evidence-Based Design, p. 194 (caption)
findings.quote: Gaze path studies show how people implicitly ignore the new Art Center in Cincinnati, Ohio, at bottom of image below, but are drawn to look at the sculpture at its entrance, and the adjacent nineteenth-century commercial building

findings.antecedent: 21st-century paradigm shift (biology/psychology)
findings.consequent: New appreciation for right hemisphere capacities (intuitive, unconscious, non-verbal)
findings.source: The Twenty-First-Century Paradigm Shift in Biology and Psychology Reframes Architecture + Its History, p. 199 (caption)
findings.quote: The unique capacities of the right hemisphere are the essence of the twenty-first-century paradigm shift, moving from the analytical and conscious thinking of the brain’s left hemisphere to acknowledge the unconscious, non-verbal capacities of the right.

findings.antecedent: Faces on book cover
findings.consequent: Visual attention/fixation (reddest heat map)
findings.source: The Twenty-First-Century Paradigm Shift in Biology and Psychology Reframes Architecture + Its History, p. 197
findings.quote: Figure 8.2 is the eye-tracked paperback version of the first edition of this book, showing how the faces on the cover at the top left draw the most attention—note the location of the reddest heat map.

findings.antecedent: Traditional Georgian house vs. modern glass building
findings.consequent: Visual attention/fixation, perceived approachability, memory formation
findings.source: The Twenty-First-Century Paradigm Shift in Biology and Psychology Reframes Architecture + Its History, p. 200
findings.quote: The heat maps (at bottom) and region of interest diagrams (in middle) predict people initially avoid looking at the glass structure almost entirely—it is implicitly ‘avoidant’—while our brain directs us to do the very opposite with the old brick one: there people focus straight on the front door!

findings.antecedent: Traditional building elevations (face-like patterns)
findings.consequent: Human well-being, sense of safety, social engagement
findings.source: The Twenty-First-Century Paradigm Shift in Biology and Psychology Reframes Architecture + Its History, p. 204
findings.quote: Traditional buildings celebrate the face-bias that promotes our species’ survival. And whether we like it or not, this remains what we still need to see to feel and be at our best in the public realm.

findings.antecedent: Founders of modern architecture with PTSD/autism
findings.consequent: Modern architectural style (unface-like, blank facades, minimal detail), difficulty for neurotypical processing, feelings of unsafety/disconnection
findings.source: The Twenty-First-Century Paradigm Shift in Biology and Psychology Reframes Architecture + Its History, p. 206
findings.quote: the paradigm for modern architecture that followed the Great War (1914–1918) reflects not only new building technologies its proponents were eager to adopt that promoted the expansive use of steel, glass, and concrete in new ways but also the distorted or damaged brain architecture of its key founders, who were WWI veterans, survivors of the first mass-industrialized military conflict the world had ever known

findings.antecedent: Walter Gropius's house design (reflecting PTSD: defensive, unface-like, minimal detail)
findings.consequent: Difficulty for neurotypical processing, lack of approachability, recreation of traumatic experience
findings.source: The Twenty-First-Century Paradigm Shift in Biology and Psychology Reframes Architecture + Its History, p. 208
findings.quote: Built in 1938, his house has a flat roof, a hidden front door, and slit windows — the better to shoot from — not unlike the bunkers Gropius would have known in the war. It says, ‘keep out, stay away!’ mirroring the defensive stance of a brain still at the Front

findings.antecedent: Autism spectrum disorder vs. neurotypical
findings.consequent: Visual fixation pattern (eyes/face vs. blankness)
findings.source: The Twenty-First-Century Paradigm Shift in Biology and Psychology Reframes Architecture + Its History, p. 214
findings.quote: typical (or neurotypical) subjects focus directly on the eyes and central area of the face in a 15-second testing interval, while a brain on the spectrum, at right, takes the opposing approach, avoiding the eyes and central face almost entirely.

findings.antecedent: Traditional carriage house (details) vs. modern library (blankness) and autism vs. neurotypical viewers
findings.consequent: Visual fixation pattern
findings.source: The Twenty-First-Century Paradigm Shift in Biology and Psychology Reframes Architecture + Its History, p. 215
findings.quote: typical subjects focus on building details, shown in heat map glowing reddest around the front door, at left, while the viewer on the spectrum, at right, fixates on building areas that are the most detail-free (Figure 8.16).

minimum_safe_summary: This expanded second edition of 'Cognitive Architecture' synthesizes findings from psychology and neuroscience to propose a new, biologically-grounded framework for architectural and urban design. It argues that human responses to the built environment are shaped by innate evolutionary traits, such as thigmotaxis (wall-hugging), a hardwired preference for faces and organized complexity, and a deep need for narrative and connection to nature (biophilia). Using biometric tools like eye-tracking, the authors demonstrate how these unconscious biases influence visual attention, emotional engagement, and spatial navigation in various architectural settings, from streetscapes to building facades. The book controversially reframes the history of modern architecture, suggesting that the 'unface-like' and minimalist designs of its founders may reflect their own underlying mental disorders (PTSD, autism) which altered their perception of visual stimuli. The core claim is that by understanding these intrinsic human behaviors, designers can create more enjoyable, healthier, and sustainable places that resonate with our evolved biological needs. The paper does not explicitly state limitations of its own methodology or findings.
